reasoning_traces.think:
The study employs Markov chains to model NFL overtime rules, distinguishing between sudden death (SD), modified sudden death (MSD), and theoretical alternatives. Each rule variant defines a unique transition matrix capturing possible game states—possession, scoring outcomes, and termination conditions. The SD model assumes immediate win upon first score, leading to a simple binary state transition. MSD introduces a restriction on the initial team’s ability to win via field goal, altering the transition probabilities. The 10-minute overtime rule modifies the time horizon and thus affects the expected number of transitions before absorption. These models enable calculation of average overtime duration and win probabilities for the first team to possess the ball. The derivation uses stochastic matrices with absorbing states to compute long-term behavior. Dualities emerge in how rule changes affect symmetry and fairness: earlier rules favored coin toss outcomes, while newer ones attempt to balance scoring opportunities. Failure modes include data insufficiency in early studies and assumption of stationary transition probabilities across seasons. The models also reveal that increasing overtime duration slightly increases average game length but decreases the first-team advantage, indicating a trade-off between fairness and game length.
